The spawning stock of Yellowtail horse mackerel (Trachurus novaezelandiae) along the southeastern Australian coast exhibits life-history traits that are tightly coupled to the cool, productive waters of the East Australian Current extension. Embryonic development is rapid, with the time at birth estimated at 10 days [ab = 10 days] when the water column registers a stable temperature of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C], a duration consistent with values reported for other carangids in temperate latitudes. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva is diminutive, carrying a wet weight at birth of only 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], a mass that reflects the small egg diameter of roughly 1 mm typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts. This tiny prolarva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during its first days of life, and the absorption of yolk nutrients must proceed rapidly at 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C] to sustain the larva until first exogenous feeding begins. The narrow thermal window appears to be critical during this lecithotrophic phase.

Juvenile recruitment to demersal habitats occurs several months after the larval pelagic phase, with recent field surveys indicating that the total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence, is 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm]. Individuals at this size weigh approximately 138 grams [Wwp = approximately 138 grams], a body mass that represents the point at which metabolic investment shifts toward reproductive activation. The allometric relationship used to derive this value, based on length-mass regressions from collected specimens, aligns closely with observations from related Trachurus species. Puberty in this species is therefore not solely a function of chronological age but is also mediated by the attainment of a threshold body size, a pattern common among iteroparous marine fishes. The length-mass conversion factor employed (0.01778) was derived from a large sample spanning the full size range of the population, ensuring that the estimated wet weight at puberty reflects the average condition of maturing individuals in this region.

The maximum recorded reproductive output for this population, extrapolated from fecundity and spawning frequency data, suggests that a mature female can achieve a daily reproduction rate of approximately 828 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 828 eggs per day] under the optimal thermal regime of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C]. This value, which is based on comparative data from the congener Trachurus picturatus, accounts for the frequency of spawning events and the number of oocytes released per event. Given that spawning occurs in multiple batches throughout the extended reproductive season, the annual reproductive investment is substantial. At this temperature, which coincides with the peak of the austral summer, the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and gamete release are met by high feeding rates on zooplankton and small pelagic crustaceans. The estimate represents a maximum potential rate and is likely moderated by local food availability and female body condition across the range.

The ultimate total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] represents the largest individuals documented in scientific surveys of Trachurus novaezelandiae, a size reached only by the oldest and most successful foragers in the population. The corresponding ultimate wet weight is 2137 grams [Wwi = 2137 grams], a body mass that reflects the species potential for significant somatic growth over its extended lifetime. This asymptotic size is achieved gradually, as growth rates slow considerably after the onset of sexual maturation and the diversion of energy toward reproductive effort. The length-mass relationship used to derive this weight follows the general form for carangids, with an exponent close to 3, indicating near-isometric scaling. Large adults of this size are most frequently encountered in offshore waters beyond the continental shelf, where prey resources are abundant and fishing pressure is lower compared to inshore nursery grounds.

Longevity data for this species, compiled from otolith-based age estimates, indicate that the maximum lifespan is 25 years [am = 25 years], a remarkable duration for a pelagic fish of this body size at a temperature of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C]. This lifespan, recorded at the prevailing water temperature of 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C], is consistent with the relatively slow life-history pace of temperate carangids and contrasts sharply with the shorter-lived, fast-growing tropical members of the genus. Such a prolonged reproductive window allows for multiple spawning seasons over the course of a lifetime, which buffers the population against occasional recruitment failures. The oldest individuals also achieve the greatest body sizes, and their contribution to the spawning stock is disproportionately important. Continued monitoring of age structure is essential for sustainable fisheries management, as the removal of these long-lived breeders could have cascading effects on the populations resilience.
